# Nāga Saṁyutta (SN 29)

**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)

**Title (Pali):** Nāga Saṁyutta

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Nāgasaṁyutta* (SN 29) is the twenty-ninth section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, grouped in Part III (the *Khandhavagga*) [Bodhi 2003; Norman 1983]. Oskar von Hinüber observes that this section preserves material scarcely related to core Buddhist doctrine but is significant for illuminating aspects of ancient Indian religion about which relatively little is known [von Hinüber 1996]. It constitutes the first of four sequential samyuttas—preceding the *Supaṇṇa-*, *Gandhabba-*, and *Valāhaka-saṁyuttas*—that examine classes of semi-celestial beings often viewed as mythological [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003_x]. According to K. R. Norman, the *Nāgasaṁyutta* contains 50 suttas, though the final 30 are preserved only in very abbreviated sketches [Norman 1983].

The central subject of the collection is the *nāga*, described as a powerful yet morally ambiguous serpentine waterway creature [SuttaCentral; Norman 1983]. In the opening discourses, the Buddha delineates the four modes of generation (*yoni*) through which *nāgas* arise: egg-born, womb-born, moisture-born, and spontaneously arisen [Bodhi 2003; Bodhi 2003_x; Hazra 1994]. The discourses enumerate the different species of *nāgas*, assess their relative superiority, and detail the courses of *kamma* that result in rebirth among them [Bodhi 2003_x; Norman 1983]. The commentary *Sāratthappakāsinī* (Spk) notes that the Buddha delivered these teachings to weary the monks of such states and rescue them from rebirth in *nāga* realms [Bodhi 2003].

Regarding text reuse and parallels, DharmaNexus demonstrates extensive internal reuse between SN 29 and its thematic companions, notably the *Gandhabbakāya Saṁyutta* (SN 31), *Valāhaka Saṁyutta* (SN 32), and *Supaṇṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 30), as well as the *Khandha Saṁyutta* (SN 22), *Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta* (SN 35), and the *Saṅkhārupapatti Sutta* (MN 120) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records parallels for three suttas in the samyutta [SuttaCentral]. In cross-language alignments, DharmaNexus detects shared passages with the Chinese *Zengyi ahan jing* (T 125), the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma work *Dharmaskandha*, the Tibetan *Saddharmānusmṛtyupasthāna*, and the *Abhidharmakośaṭīkā* [DharmaNexus].
